presentingComplaint: Two days of intermittent black, tarry stools and a single small coffee-ground vomit, without collapse or ongoing brisk bleeding.
history: Known alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh A, MELD low) diagnosed 2 years ago, abstinent for 6 months. He noticed dark tarry stools over the last 48 hours and this morning brought up a small amount of coffee-ground material once. He feels mildly light-headed on standing but has not fainted, has had no fresh haematemesis, and has continued taking oral fluids and a light diet. No NSAID or anticoagulant use, no prior documented ulcer. A surveillance endoscopy 8 months earlier had shown small (grade I) oesophageal varices on non-selective beta-blocker prophylaxis (carvedilol), which he admits to taking irregularly. No fever, abdominal pain, jaundice or confusion.
examination: Alert, orientated, comfortable at rest. Mild conjunctival pallor. No asterixis, no jaundice. A few spider naevi over the chest and palmar erythema. Abdomen soft, non-tender; spleen tip palpable 2 cm below costal margin; no clinically detectable ascites. Rectal examination confirms melaena. No stigmata of active large-volume bleeding; peripheries warm, capillary refill <2 s.
imaging: Bedside ultrasound: coarse, nodular liver with splenomegaly (14 cm) and patent, mildly dilated portal vein consistent with portal hypertension; trace perihepatic fluid only, no gross ascites.
microbiology: Not applicable; no features of infection. Blood cultures not indicated on clinical grounds.
finalDiagnosis: Acute variceal bleeding - small-volume, haemodynamically stable (early/mild) presentation in compensated alcohol-related cirrhosis, confirmed as a recent variceal bleed at endoscopy.
citations: Baveno VII - Portal Hypertension and Variceal Bleeding - 2022
AASLD - Portal Hypertensive Bleeding in Cirrhosis - 2016
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e - Cirrhosis and Portal Hypertension
stewardship: Non-infective diagnosis. Note: current guidelines recommend short-course prophylactic antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone) for any cirrhotic patient with acute GI bleeding, but this case is coded non-infective; empiric therapy is captured narratively rather than as a stewardship tier.
contraindications: Avoid over-transfusion - target restrictive haemoglobin threshold ~7 g/dL (transfuse to 7-8 g/dL) as over-transfusion raises portal pressure and rebleeding risk
Avoid excessive crystalloid volume resuscitation for the same reason
Beta-blocker should be withheld during the acute bleed while assessing haemodynamics
edgeCases: Mild presentation can be falsely reassuring - early endoscopy (within 24 h) is still required as small varices can rebleed
Urea elevated out of proportion to creatinine supports an upper-GI source even without haematemesis
Thrombocytopenia and splenomegaly point to portal hypertension rather than a simple peptic ulcer
Beta-blocker may blunt the expected tachycardia, masking blood loss
expectedMaiK: Suspect acute variceal bleeding in any cirrhotic with melaena/haematemesis even when haemodynamically stable; risk-stratify, start vasoactive therapy (terlipressin/octreotide) and prophylactic antibiotics, and arrange early upper GI endoscopy for band ligation.
expectedNextQuestions: Volume and frequency of melaena and any fresh haematemesis?
Postural symptoms, syncope or ongoing light-headedness?
Adherence to non-selective beta-blocker and last surveillance endoscopy findings?
Alcohol intake, NSAID/anticoagulant use and prior bleeding episodes?
expectedInvestigations: Urgent upper GI endoscopy within 24 hours (diagnostic and for band ligation)
FBC, coagulation profile (INR), U&E, LFTs and group-and-save/crossmatch
Assess Child-Pugh / MELD for prognosis and rebleeding risk

investigations: Urgent upper GI endoscopy within 24 hours with band ligation
